c_open: We used to throw stones into that corner. ... And the corner would throw them back.
c_s1: We'd been in that building fifteen years. Repairing grass-cutting machinery. Ordinary place. [exhales] Then stones started coming across the workshop. Little stones, pinging off the machinery. We thought — kids. But there were no kids round there. There was no chance of anybody being in that shop except us three. That's when I started to worry about that building.
c_s2: You never saw them in the air. You'd hear it hit the wall, hear it drop... you'd look round, and there's the stone, sat on the floor. And one corner of the shop would go ice cold. My wife felt it first. [pause] Then money started turning up. A fiver, folded, pushed up under a ceiling tile. ... Like it was paying rent.
c_s3: We wrote to the Society for Psychical Research, in London. They sent a professor of psychology. And as that man walked through our door — his first minute in the shop — a stone came across the room and went off a piece of machinery. [soft laugh] I said, see? That's Pete. He's saying hello. ... That professor kept coming back for two years.
c_s4: Well, you had to call it something. Pete. [exhales] And we were never really afraid of it, that's the honest truth. It became part of the family. People think that's the strange part — that we weren't frightened. ... But they weren't there for the corner.
c_s5: The professor did an experiment. He'd throw a stone into the cold corner. And it would come back. Not bounce back. Come back. Thrown. [pause] He wrote it up for the Society. Said it had intent. Rudimentary intelligence — those were his words. [exhales] A stone comes back at you out of an empty corner, and you understand — it's not a draught. Something in that corner was deciding. ... He never found a trick. And I never found out what we'd shared that building with, all those years.
